title: Getting to Yes
db_title_note: DB: 'Müzakerede Evet Almak' by Roger Fisher (1981); the book is Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury (Bruce Patton joined in later editions). No primary text readable; facts come from study guides, medium confidence.

facts.claim: Getting to Yes, Roger Fisher and William Ury, first published 1981. Four principles: separate people from the problem, focus on interests not positions, invent options for mutual gain, insist on objective criteria.
Library window: two men argue in a library, one wants the window open, the other closed (no draft). The librarian opens a window in the next room: fresh air without a draft.

Camp David 1978: Israel wanted to keep part of the Sinai, Egypt wanted all of it back. Israel's interest was security (no Egyptian forces massed near its border); Egypt's was sovereignty. Outcome: Sinai returned to Egypt under a demilitarization condition.

Method: ask why you want something and why the other side does not; the authors say people often identify a cause, not a purpose, when asked why. Basic interests listed: security, economic well-being, sense of belonging, recognition, control over one's life.
The authors coined the term BATNA, 'best alternative to a negotiated agreement'.

'The reason you negotiate is to produce something better than the results you can obtain without negotiating.' The BATNA is the standard against which an offer is measured; the authors treat it as the main source of a negotiator's power, rather than money or influence.
facts.source: litcharts BATNA entry, study-guide quoting the book

facts.claim: Chapter title: 'What If They Are More Powerful? (Develop Your BATNA)'.

Objective criteria chapter: negotiators should rest agreements on fair standards such as market value, replacement cost, precedent, scientific judgment, professional standards, efficiency, reciprocity. 'Yield to principle, not to pressure.'

Law of the Sea Conference: the U.S. and India disagreed on whether mining companies should pay a fee to start mining. After looking at an economic model developed at MIT, both reconsidered and neither had to back down.
Fair procedures: dividing a dessert, 'one cuts, the other chooses' gives the cutter a reason to cut evenly; also taking turns, drawing lots, letting a third party decide.
Reciprocity test: ask whether the other side would accept the same terms if positions were reversed.
